summary: History-of-science topic for ages 9-11: ideas about what sits at the centre of the solar system changed as evidence accumulated. Learners contrast the geocentric model (Earth fixed at the centre, Ptolemy) with the heliocentric model (Sun at the centre, proposed by Copernicus), and examine Galileo's telescope evidence from c.1610 — four moons circling Jupiter and the phases of Venus — that supported the Sun-centred picture. Two teaching goals: (1) contrast the two models, and (2) show that science advances by testing ideas against evidence, so models are held, challenged and revised rather than simply believed. Start from why geocentrism was reasonable (the sky really does appear to go around us), keep Galileo's telescope evidence as the pivot, and make the nature-of-science lesson explicit.
misconceptions: Thinking the geocentric model was just 'stupid' — not appreciating it matched the everyday appearance of the sky and was carefully worked out, which is why it lasted so long.
Believing Copernicus or Galileo 'proved' heliocentrism single-handedly and instantly, rather than it being a gradual accumulation of evidence and acceptance over time.
Thinking Galileo INVENTED the telescope or the heliocentric idea, rather than improving the telescope and providing evidence for Copernicus's model.
Assuming scientific ideas are fixed facts handed down, missing the core lesson that models change when new evidence appears.
Confusing 'the Sun appears to move across the sky' (an appearance caused by Earth's spin) with the Sun actually orbiting Earth.
Believing everyone accepted the new model at once, ignoring the real resistance from common sense and authority.

activities.title: Two sky-machines, side by side: which model fits the evidence?
steps: Study two diagrams of the same sky objects arranged differently: one Earth-centred (Ptolemy, geocentric), one Sun-centred (Copernicus, heliocentric).
Use a 'Galileo's telescope, 1610' view aimed at Jupiter and advance night by night; watch four tiny points of light shuffle back and forth, always strung out beside Jupiter.
State in your own words what those four moons show: they orbit Jupiter, so it cannot be true that everything circles the Earth.
Assign that observation to each model and judge which one accounts for it — the Sun-centred arrangement works, the strict 'everything orbits Earth' claim breaks.
Advance the view to Venus over successive observations and watch it cycle through a full set of phases; decide which model this clue best fits.
Say which model the evidence supports and why a long-held idea gave way.
activities.insight: Scientists' minds began to change, over many years, because new evidence (Jupiter's moons and Venus's phases) could not be explained by Ptolemy's Earth-centred model, in which everything circles Earth; models are tested against observation, not merely believed.

activities.title: Interview Galileo (and Copernicus): why change your mind?
steps: Talk in role to Galileo on the night of 1610 he first sees Jupiter's moons: ask 'what did you see?', 'how do you know they orbit Jupiter?', and 'why don't people believe you?'
Optionally interview Copernicus on why he moved the Sun to the centre.
Capture, in your own words, the evidence Galileo gives and the resistance he met.
Explain why changing a long-held, authority-backed idea was hard — it clashed with common sense and with accepted authority.
activities.insight: The shift to a Sun-centred model was a human story: it rested on evidence and met real resistance, showing how science advances through argument over evidence.

activities.title: Then-and-now: labelled models, timeline and the Jupiter observation
steps: Reveal the label on each model: geocentric diagram → 'Earth at centre, Ptolemy'; heliocentric diagram → 'Sun at centre, Copernicus'.
Reveal the Jupiter observation → four orbiting moons and the point 'so not everything orbits Earth'.
Order a simple timeline: ancient geocentric → Copernicus (1500s) → Galileo's telescope evidence (c.1610).
Attach each name to its role: Ptolemy = influential geocentric model; Copernicus = proposed Sun-centred; Galileo = telescope evidence supporting it.
activities.insight: The labelled pair, timeline and reveals are intended to help learners attach the models, the names and the key evidence to one another and see the chronological development of the ideas.

activities.title: Check and explain: who proposed what, and what the evidence showed
steps: Match each person to their model or contribution (Ptolemy, Copernicus, Galileo).
Answer 'what did Jupiter's moons show?' and explain the reasoning, not just pick the fact.
Sequence the timeline of ideas from ancient geocentrism to Galileo's evidence.
Respond to the prompt: 'Were the ancients simply foolish, or did the Earth-centred idea make sense from what they could see? What evidence helped change people's minds? Tell me WHY.'
activities.insight: Learners can both recall the roles/evidence and articulate why geocentrism was reasonable and how evidence drove the change — distinguishing reciting names from grasping evidence-driven model change.

activities.title: Optional: view each model in space with a 3D orrery
steps: Switch a 3D orrery between the Earth-centred and Sun-centred arrangements and view each from different angles.
Relate the spatial layout back to the deciding evidence you already examined (Jupiter's moons orbiting Jupiter, Venus's phases).
activities.insight: Seeing each model as a spatial arrangement can reinforce the contrast between the two layouts for some learners.

checkQuestion: For a very long time, intelligent people were certain the Sun and planets all went around a still Earth. Were they simply being foolish, or did it make sense from what they could see? And what finally convinced people that the Earth goes round the Sun instead? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: They weren't foolish. The Earth-centred (geocentric) idea, set out by Ptolemy, fitted everyday experience really well: we don't feel the Earth moving, and the Sun, Moon and stars all APPEAR to cross the sky each day as if going around us. Copernicus proposed the Sun-centred (heliocentric) model, but what changed people's minds was new EVIDENCE: when Galileo turned his telescope to the sky he saw things the old model couldn't explain — four moons orbiting Jupiter (so not everything orbits Earth) and the changing phases of Venus. The story shows scientific ideas change when new evidence arrives, not because earlier people were stupid.
